🐛 Describe the bug
This bug report is created based on this thread on the PyTorch Forums:
"Torch._dynamo hit config.cache_size_limit when adding LR scheduler"
It is observed that the duration of a batch training step, compiled with torch.compile, takes longer to converge when adding an LR scheduler to the end of the step function. For some reason it seems that more compilations are cached.
Tagging @msaroufim on request.
Error logs
There are no errors, but warnings that signal that there is an issue, also see the PyTorch forum thread as mentioned above:

🐛 Describe the bug
In #105044, support for HF ModelOutput was moved from DataClassVariable to CustomizedDictVariable. However, the new implementation didn't consider the ModelOutput behavior of 'when value is None, only set it as attribute, but skip updating it in dict' as defined in their custom __setattr__:
# class ModelOutput
    def __setattr__(self, name, value):
        if name in self.keys() and value is not None:
            # Don't call self.__setitem__ to avoid recursion errors
            super().__setitem__(name, value)
        super().__setattr__(name, value)
Hence all items whose values are None are ignored during to_tuple and __getitem__(idx: int). Where on the contrary dynamo traced graph will not ignore None values. This behavior was noted and covered in previous DataClassVariable implementation.

  
    
      pytorch/torch/_dynamo/variables/dicts.py
    
    
        Lines 350 to 354
      in
      a75de6d
    
  
  
    

        
          
           if cls.include_none: 
        

        
          
               assert variables.ConstantVariable.is_literal(val) 
        

        
          
               items[key] = variables.ConstantVariable(val) 
        

        
          
           else: 
        

        
          
               assert val is None, f"unexpected {val}" 
        
    
  


This leads to incorrect traced graphs when user code does the combination of setting None attributes and accessing via to_tuple or getitem via index.
This is discovered from huggingface Llava model.
Repro:
import torch
import transformers
from transformers import file_utils  # Crucial, otherwise dynamo fails.
from transformers.modeling_outputs import CausalLMOutputWithPast

class Model(torch.nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        x = x + 1
        return CausalLMOutputWithPast(loss=None, logits=x)[0]

model = Model()
x = torch.randn(1, 1, 1, 1)
eo = torch._dynamo.export(Model(), aten_graph=True)(x)
eo.graph_module.print_readable()
print("dynamo output: ", eo.graph_module(x))
print("eager output: ", model(x))

dynamo output:  None
eager output:  tensor([[[[-0.4403]]]])

Parametrization injects a property onto the parametrized module that returns a nn.Module() that, when evaluated on a module parameter, returns a "reparametrized" module parameter. Dynamo tries to lift the returned tensor to be a graph input, but as it's temporary, the lookup within tensor_weakref_to_sizes_strides fails later on during guard generation.

🐛 Describe the bug
I have encountered an issue with the torch.clamp function in PyTorch when it is used on tensors that reside on the Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) device. Specifically, the function behaves differently with NaN values on tensors across different devices (mps vs. cpu/cuda). This inconsistency can lead to unexpected results when working with NaN values on MPS devices.
When using torch.clamp on a tensor with NaN values on an MPS device, If both min and max parameters are set, the function replaces NaN values with the min value. If only one of min and max parameters are set, the function replaces NaN values with the min value. If only one of the min and max parameters is set, the function replaces NaN values with the specified min or max parameter.
This behavior is inconsistent with how torch.clamp operates on the same tensor when it is on a CPU device, where NaN values remain unchanged.
import torch

t_mps = torch.tensor([torch.nan, 1, 2], device="mps")
print(torch.clamp(t_mps, min=-100, max=100))
# tensor([-100.,    1.,    2.], device='mps:0')
print(torch.clamp(t_mps, min=-100))
# tensor([-100.,    1.,    2.], device='mps:0')
print(torch.clamp(t_mps, max=100))
# tensor([100.,   1.,   2.], device='mps:0')

t_cpu = torch.tensor([torch.nan, 1, 2], device="cpu")
print(torch.clamp(t_cpu, min=-100, max=100))
# tensor([nan, 1., 2.])
print(torch.clamp(t_cpu, min=-100))
# tensor([nan, 1., 2.])
print(torch.clamp(t_cpu, max=100))
# tensor([nan, 1., 2.])
Expected Behavior:
The behavior of torch.clamp should be consistent across different devices. When dealing with NaN values, torch.clamp should not replace NaN values.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
moving from slack discussion
How can FSDP shard a model directly to GPUs during model instantiation?
This is critical for instantiating huge models.
Alternatives
In Deepspeed this exists since day 0 of the framework using zero.Init
This feature is integrated into HF Transformers' from_pretrained that instantiates the model directly on GPUs - here
There is an emerging need to control when this should be activated and when
not as we now have many situations with multiple concurrent models and this
current setup no longer works well.So I thought that HF Transformers should
gather at least some needs of various frameworks - Deepspeed ZeRO, FSDP and
may be others where from_pretrained provides hooks into the model
instantiation stage. The 2 needs are:

yes/no activate flag
framework provided context to instantiate in - so zero.Init would be just one of them

The intention is that the user won't need to do anything special when they
create the model. The framework would register with HF Transformers everything
it needs to do it smoothly and correctly.
Additional context
on slack Andrew Gu posted:

If you specify the  device_id arg, FSDP should move the unsharded module to GPU before sharding so that the sharding ops are fast (but still requiring CPU init and copy H2D). Otherwise, the only other way to initialize and shard on GPU is to do so-called “manual wrapping”, which was the common approach from Fairscale. I do not think that would work with HF transformers.


For manual wrapping, you have to call FullyShardedDataParallel(module, …) on
module immediately after it was constructed to avoid spiking memory. This is
intrusive to the model definition and not acceptable in many cases. I am just
mentioning it since it can be the fastest init supported.

# Example manual wrapping with `enable_wrap`/`wrap`
# Wrap each transformer block and the root
from torch.distributed.fsdp import enable_wrap, wrap

class Transformer(nn.Module):
  def __init__(self, ...):
    layers = []
    for layer_id in range(num_layers):
      layer = TransformerBlock(...)
      layer = wrap(layer, ...)
      layers.append(layer)
    self.layers = nn.ModuleList(layers)
    
with torch.device("cuda"):
  with enable_wrap(wrapper_cls=FullyShardedDataParallel, **fsdp_kwargs):
    model = Transformer(...)
    wrap(model)

cc @zhaojuanmao @mrshenli @rohan-varma @awgu @fegin @penguinwu @kwen2501

from typing import List

import torch


E4M3_MAX_POS = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
E5M2_MAX_POS = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e5m2).max
EPS = 1e-12

SIZES = [torch.Size([1152, 768]), torch.Size([384, 768])]


def to_fp8_saturated(x, float8_dtype: torch.dtype):
    if float8_dtype == torch.float8_e4m3fn:
        x = x.clamp(min=-1 * E4M3_MAX_POS, max=E4M3_MAX_POS)
    else:
        x = x.clamp(min=-1 * E5M2_MAX_POS, max=E5M2_MAX_POS)
    return x.to(float8_dtype)


def inner_fn(weights: List[torch.Tensor]):
    # All-reduce partial amaxes computed from sharded weights
    abs_weights = torch._foreach_abs(weights)
    partial_amax_tensor = abs_weights[0].new_empty(len(abs_weights))
    for i, abs_weight in enumerate(abs_weights):
        torch.max(abs_weight, out=partial_amax_tensor[i])
    # NOTE: The error reproduces without this all-reduce, so let us use a
    # single-GPU repro.
    # replicated_amax_tensor = torch.distributed._functional_collectives.all_reduce(
    #     partial_amax_tensor, "MAX", list(range(torch.distributed.get_world_size()))
    # )
    replicated_amax_tensor = partial_amax_tensor

    # Compute scales from replicated amaxes and the fp8 bit datas
    clamped_tensor = torch.clamp(replicated_amax_tensor, EPS)
    scales_tensor = E4M3_MAX_POS / clamped_tensor
    datas = []
    scales = []
    for i, weight in enumerate(weights):
        scale = scales_tensor[i]
        weight_scaled = weight * scale
        datas.append(to_fp8_saturated(weight_scaled, torch.float8_e4m3fn))
        scales.append(scale)
    return datas, scales


weights = [torch.randn(size, device="cuda") for size in SIZES]

🐛 Describe the bug
I am using a custom python based store to address the issue of torch's TCPStore running out of file handle resources when running on a large number of GPUs. However, torch by default wraps the store into a PrefixStore which seems to disable the python API.
I am getting the following error
L ASSERT FAILED at "/gpfs/alpine2/bif143/proj-shared/summit_py310/conda-bld/pytorch-base_1708839867265/work/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/init.cpp":151, please report a bug to PyTorch. Not implemented.
Exception raised from get at /gpfs/alpine2/bif143/proj-shared/summit_py310/conda-bld/pytorch-base_1708839867265/work/torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/init.cpp:151 (most recent call first):
frame #0: c10::Error::Error(c10::SourceLocation, std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> >) + 0xfc (0x200072d39d3c in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libc10.so)
frame #1: c10::detail::torchCheckFail(char const*, char const*, unsigned int, std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&) + 0x124 (0x200072cd1d04 in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libc10.so)
frame #2: c10::detail::torchInternalAssertFail(char const*, char const*, unsigned int, char const*, char const*) + 0x70 (0x200072d363e0 in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libc10.so)
frame #3: <unknown function> + 0xe74814 (0x2000429a4814 in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_python.so)
frame #4: c10d::PrefixStore::get(std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&) + 0x6c (0x20004993f4bc in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_cpu.so)
frame #5: c10d::PrefixStore::get(std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&) + 0x6c (0x20004993f4bc in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_cpu.so)
frame #6: c10d::ProcessGroupNCCL::broadcastUniqueNCCLID(ncclUniqueId*, bool, std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&, int) + 0x234 (0x20004df5e7e4 in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_cuda.so)
frame #7: c10d::ProcessGroupNCCL::getNCCLComm(std::__cxx11::basic_string<char, std::char_traits<char>, std::allocator<char> > const&, std::vector<c10::Device, std::allocator<c10::Device> > const&, c10d::OpType, int, bool) + 0x294 (0x20004df64a44 in /gpfs/alpine2/proj-shared/bif143/summit_py310/lib/python3.10/site-packages/torch/lib/libtorch_cuda.so)

implying that the torch can't resolve the virtual overload of the Store->get() function, even though it is implemented in the custom store.
My store:
from mpi4py import MPI
import torch.distributed as dist

class MPIStore(dist.Store):
    def __init__(self, comm=None):
        super().__init__()
        self.comm = comm
        if self.comm is None:
            self.comm = MPI.COMM_WORLD

    # Function to get value associated with a key
    def get(self, key):
        return self.comm.bcast(None)

    # Function to put a key-value pair into the store
    def set(self, key, value):
        self.comm.bcast(value)

    def add(self, key, value):
        return self.comm.Get_size()

    def wait(self, keys, timeout):
        pass

if __name__ == '__main__':
    dist._test_python_store(dist.PrefixStore('prefix', MPIStore()))

(i.e. just replace the complicated key/value store logic by a simple brodcast to set up NCCL)
Current output of this reproducer:
$ jsrun -n 1 python mpi_store.py 
Warning: OMP_NUM_THREADS=16 is greater than available PU's
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/gpfs/alpine2/bif143/proj-shared/glaser/affinity_clip/affinity_clip/mpi_store.py", line 26, in <module>
    dist._test_python_store(dist.PrefixStore('prefix', MPIStore()))
RuntimeError: Tried to call pure virtual function "::c10d::Store::add"

Expected output:
TypeError: Object of type 'NoneType' is not an instance of 'bytes'

(yes, that is an error, too, but it is expected from running this somewhat hacky class in a unit test setting rather than inside the distributed communication setup)
Workaround:
torch.distributed.distributed_c10d.PrefixStore = lambda x, s: s
torch.distributed.init_process_group("nccl",
                                     store=MPIStore(),
                                     rank=comm.Get_rank(),
                                     world_size=comm.Get_size())

i.e. monkey patch the PrefixStore to be a no-op.
It would be nice if PrefixStore could be updated to accept custom Python stores.
To address the underlying issue of distributed setup, it should be possible to initialize NCCL using MPI communicators instead of using TCP. Perhaps revamping the logic behind the k/v stores and reducing them to a bcast call might help here, if it applies to all other back ends as well.
Versions
tested with 2.0

📚 The doc issue
The scaled-dot-product-attention doc claims
attn_mask (optional Tensor) – Attention mask; shape (N,...,L,S). 

However, if we try the attached broadcast-mask.py.zip, we will see
query shape = torch.Size([3, 2, 4, 7, 16])
key shape = torch.Size([3, 2, 4, 5, 16])
value shape = torch.Size([3, 2, 4, 5, 32])
mask shape = torch.Size([1, 1, 5])
attention shape = torch.Size([3, 2, 4, 7, 32])

This means our real shape requirement for attn_mask is (..., S) and broadcastable to (N, ..., L, S)
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Please update the scaled-dot-product-attention doc so it is consistent with the code behavior.
Or, if the code behavior is to-be-changed to conform to doc, please either raise exception in code or mark deprecation warning.
cc @svekars @brycebortree @jbschlosser @bhosmer @cpuhrsch @erichan1 @drisspg @mikaylagawarecki

🐛 Describe the bug
While debugging some accuracy issues with a custom triton kernel with autotune configs running inside a torch.compile() environment, I've noticed that when the kernel has a few configs available defined through @triton.autotune(), the results will be wrong for the first run (when autotune is supposed to run).
While digging deep into how these kernels get put into the inductor codegen path, I've noticed that while inductor-generated kernels have mutated_args as part of their inductor_meta properties, custom kernels lack this parameter, which cached_autotune will use to prevent the issue I'm talking about from happening.
If I understand the rest of the code correctly, this seems to stem from the custom triton kernel getting functionalized in the AOT autograd step, so maybe the issue is there. nodes.title: Custom triton kernels with autotune running in torch.compile() don't seem to properly capture mutating inputs

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
As title says, when using a custom Triton kernel inside a torch.compile() environment, if it gets called twice with inputs of different shapes, the grid computation will be wrong for all calls except for the last one. While inspecting the inductor codegen code, I've identified a few issues:

For a triton kernel named fused_moe_kernel, inductor codegen will generate a grid_wrapper_for_fused_moe_kernel_0. The first issue is that this will get generated for every single call to fused_moe_kernel in the graph, with the same name. Of course, given some calls require different grid sizes, this is going to fail.
When investigating why this might be the case, I saw that define_user_defined_triton_kernel and generate_user_defined_triton_kernel only cache the kernel based on the input dtypes and not their shapes, which means a single grid function name is created for all calls.

I hope this is enough to track down the issue. If necessary, I can write a repro later in the week.

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Motivation
SPMD sharding in pytorch/XLA offers model parallelism by sharding tensors within an operator. However, we need a mechanism to integrate this capapability with pipeline parallelism for models that are large and cannot use SPMD sharding (using mark_sharding APIs) either for performance reasons or memory constraints.
Pitch
The high level idea is to integrate the pipeline parallel functionality of the existing package with GSPMD
https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/libraries/neuronx-distributed/pipeline_parallelism_overview.html
As described in the docs,
“In NeuronxDistributed, we use Pytorch’s FX to trace the model and do partition on the FX IR. User simply needs to specify where to cut the pipeline stages, and our algorithm will cut the pipeline stages and assign the corresponding modules to each Neuron core automatically.”
Alternatives
No response
Additional context

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
import math

def naive_sdp2(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    attn_scores = torch.matmul(Q, K.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(Q.size(-1))
    if mask is not None:
        attn_scores = attn_scores.masked_fill(mask == 0, -1e9)
    attn_probs = torch.softmax(attn_scores, dim=-1)
    output = torch.matmul(attn_probs, V)
    return output

query = torch.rand(1, 32, 1024, 64, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
key = torch.rand(1, 32, 1024, 64, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
value = torch.rand(1, 32, 1024, 64, dtype=torch.bfloat16)

Q = query.view(query.size(0) * query.size(1), query.size(2), query.size(3))

K = key.view(key.size(0) * key.size(1), key.size(2), key.size(3))

V = value.view(value.size(0) * value.size(1), value.size(2), value.size(3))

import time
repeat_time = 100
total_time = 0
for i in range(repeat_time):
    start_time = time.time()
    naive_sdp2(Q, K, V)
    total_time += time.time() - start_time

print(f"attn total time:{total_time}s, avg time: {total_time / repeat_time}s")

total_time = 0
for i in range(repeat_time):
   start_time = time.time()
   F.scaled_dot_product_attention(query,key,value)
   total_time += time.time() - start_time
print(f"fa total time:{total_time}s, avg time: {total_time / repeat_time}s")

🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
For implementing things like Alibi, we need a tensor in our model that is the same on each rank, is small, and never changes. This is very hard to do in FSDP.
It would be easiest if I could write this:
class MyModel(nn.Module):
    my_static_tensor = torch.randn(1,2,3)
Or maybe a little more practical:
class MyModel(nn.Module):
    my_static_tensor = MyModel.make_my_static_Tensor()

    @staticmethod
    def make_my_static_tensor():
        # do whatever
        return torch.randn(1,2,3)
I need to somehow indicate that my_static_tensor should never be touched by FSDP.
Alternatives
In the OLMo codebase we did this to hide these tensors from FSDP: https://github.com/allenai/OLMo/blob/922db6aa17ec05de9f4d8e6e9799f80384021dc4/olmo/model.py#L91
This is annoying and required us to pass around an instance of BufferCache everywhere.
Additional context
There is some helpful context in the doc string for our BufferCache class:
    """
    Cache for attention biases and other things that would normally be stored as buffers.
    We avoid using buffers because we've run into various issues doing so with FSDP.
    In general it appears the way FSDP handles buffers is not well-defined.
    It doesn't shard them but apparently it does synchronize them across processes, which we want to avoid
    since (A) it isn't necessary, and (B) we sometimes have `-inf` in these biases which might get turned into
    NaNs when they're synchronized due to casting or some other issue.
    """

🐛 Describe the bug
Hi,
I'm doing experiments with distributed training with torch (related to this). I found that when I'm training my model on two hosts (on any number of hosts > 1) DtoH operations have significant impact on collective communications (in particular, AG).
Below is the overall trace from 16 GPU (2 hosts) which shows what I'm talking about:

The trace was obtained with the following code (After ranks and other torch.distributed setup):
    from torch.profiler import schedule
    my_schedule = schedule( # just setup scheduler 
    skip_first=1,
    wait=1,
    warmup=1,
    active=58,
    repeat=1)

    n_gpus = torch.distributed.get_world_size()
    print(f"Running on {n_gpus} gpus")
    W = 8192*4
    H = 8192*4
    # large cuda tensor
    activation_tensor = torch.rand(W, H, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=torch.device('cuda'))
    # large cuda tensor 
    weight_tensor = torch.rand(W, H//n_gpus, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=torch.device('cuda'))
    cpu_buffer = torch.empty(W, H, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device='cpu', pin_memory=True)
    to_tensor = torch.zeros_like(activation_tensor)
    N_times = 30 # how many times to run each kernel (loops)
    comm_stream = torch.cuda.Stream(priority=-1)
    offload_stream = torch.cuda.Stream()
    torch.distributed.barrier() # just to start from here simultaneously
    torch.cuda.synchronize() # wait all

    with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA], record_shapes=True,schedule=my_schedule) as prof:
        for op_idx in range(N_times):
            with torch.cuda.stream(comm_stream):
                torch.distributed.all_gather_into_tensor(to_tensor, weight_tensor)
            with torch.cuda.stream(offload_stream):
                cpu_buffer.copy_(activation_tensor, non_blocking=True) # Here is DtoH

            prof.step()
        torch.cuda.synchronize() # wait all kernels in all streams

        for op_idx_1 in range(N_times):
            with torch.cuda.stream(comm_stream):
                torch.distributed.reduce_scatter_tensor(weight_tensor, to_tensor)
                torch.distributed.all_gather_into_tensor(to_tensor, weight_tensor)
            with torch.cuda.stream(offload_stream):
                activation_tensor.copy_(cpu_buffer, non_blocking=True) # Here is HtoD

            prof.step()
        torch.cuda.synchronize() # wait all kernels in all streams

Here I noticed that the first loop (AG + DtoH)  looks bizarre:

Here is about 606ms per AG, but for the second loop with the same AG, but with HtoD (btw, thus, the load on a bus is approximately the same during that second loop) looks like this:

i.e. 25ms per AG, which is about 40 times slowdown for AG with DtoH.
So the question of this issue is why there is so significant slowdown when using DtoH in another stream?
P.S.
For the same experiment with one host only there is no such unusual effect.
I use IB-connection between hosts.

🐛 Describe the bug
In https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/torch/_dynamo/eval_frame.py , there is a code snippet:
if TYPE_CHECKING:
    from torch._C._dynamo.eval_frame import (  # noqa: F401
        reset_code,
        set_eval_frame,
        set_guard_error_hook,
        skip_code,
        unsupported,
    )
else:
    for name in dir(torch._C._dynamo.eval_frame):
        if name.startswith("__"):
            continue
        globals()[name] = getattr(torch._C._dynamo.eval_frame, name)
There are two problems with this code snippet:

Imported names are not the same: with TYPE_CHECKING, we import reset_code/set_eval_frame/set_guard_error_hook/skip_code/unsupported, but without TYPE_CHECKING, we would additionally import _CacheEntry/_ExtraState/_debug_get_cache_entry_list.
Misleading code: with TYPE_CHECKING, it seems we can use from torch._C._dynamo.eval_frame import set_eval_frame. However, the code is in fact illegal, as torch._C._dynamo is not a package.

Maybe we can modify the code under TYPE_CHECKING to avoid these problems, such as reset_code = torch._C._dynamo.eval_frame.reset_code.
Would like to hear opinions from @jansel @ezyang and so on. If it is doable, I can submit a corresponding PR to fix it.

Example trivial subclass implementing __torch_function__(). Note dynamic=True and the call to composite op unflatten() in the compiled function.
In the torch_function impl: with torch._C.DisableTorchFunctionSubclass() for redispatch breaks Proxy.
import torch
import torch.utils._pytree as pytree

class SubTensor(torch.Tensor):
    @staticmethod
    def __new__(cls, t):
        return torch.Tensor._make_wrapper_subclass(
            cls, t.shape, t.stride(), t.storage_offset(), torch.contiguous_format, t.dtype,
            torch.strided, t.device, False, t.requires_grad, "sizes", False, False, None
        )

    def __init__(self, t):
        super().__init__()
        self._t = t

    def __tensor_flatten__(self):
        return ["_t"], {}

    @staticmethod
    def __tensor_unflatten__(inner_tensors, ctx, outer_size, outer_stride):
        t = inner_tensors["_t"]
        return SubTensor(t)

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"SubTensor({self._t})"

    @classmethod
    def __torch_function__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        if kwargs is None:
            kwargs = {}

        with torch._C.DisableTorchFunctionSubclass():
            return func(*args, **kwargs)

    @classmethod
    def __torch_dispatch__(cls, func, types, args=(), kwargs=None):
        kwargs = {} if kwargs is None else kwargs
        new_args = pytree.tree_map_only(SubTensor, lambda s: s._t, args)
        output = func(*new_args, **kwargs)
        output = pytree.tree_map_only(torch.Tensor, lambda t: SubTensor(t), output)
        return output


@torch.compile(dynamic=True)
def f(x):
    return x.unflatten(-1, [2, 5])

nodes.bodyText:
🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch
Consider the following statement
torch_array = torch.tensor(other_array)
where other_array is an array instance constructed by another array programming framework. If this other framework is principally designed around the DLPack array exchange protocol, something very bad happens.
Basically PyTorch ignores the DLPack interface (other_array.__dlpack__) altogether. Furthermore, if other_array exposes the sequence protocol (__len__ and __getitem__), PyTorch will perform a brute-force element-wise copy potentially requiring hundreds of millions of separate PCI-express transactions to copy individual floating point values from the GPU. To the user, it will seem that the application has crashed because nothing happens and attempting to interrupt the Python kernel doesn't work since this is all done on the C++ side.
Fortunately PyTorch supports the DLPack protocol to efficiently exchange tensors with other libraries. But it only does so when the user creates the arrays in a sort of awkward way:
from torch.utils.dlpack import from_dlpack
torch_array = from_dlpack(other_array)
It's easy to forget to do this, with extremely unpleasant results. It would be very easy easy for PyTorch to check if other_array implements the DLPack protocol and then simply to switch to this construction method. I will create a separate PR proposing a prototype of this idea.
Alternatives
N/A
Additional context
No response

🐛 Describe the bug
FX graph recompilations happening due the substitution of hint value with the symbolic variable. It seems, dynamic FX graphs is not getting reused in this case.
For example, Consider testcase with 3 iteration of dynamic input shapes.
First iteration run with static variables. In the second iteration, dynamicity is detect and symbolic variables are created. But the symbolic variables are replaced with hint value.
Due this, the third iteration performed FX recompilation and followed the similar symbolic variable replacement with hint values.

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
Hi,
We find the user stream instance outside the torch.compile scope can not be captured by dynamo, thus when the stream methods are called, the torch.compile crashed because the stream instance is None in the dynamo graph and it can not be constructed as a stream variable in the dynamo.
The motivation for the issue is that the distributed framework like FSDP/DeepSpeed will use stream methods to sync between the computation stream and the communication stream. Taking graph break into the consideration, the stream instance may be created outside the subgraph, where the stream methods are called.
Here is the reproducer:
import torch
stream1 = torch.cuda.Stream()
stream2 = torch.cuda.Stream()

@torch.compile(backend='inductor')
def test(x):
    with torch.cuda.stream(stream1):
        x = x + 2.0
    stream2.wait_stream(stream1)
    with torch.cuda.stream(stream2):
        x = x + 3.0
    return x

input = torch.ones(3, 3, device='cuda')
output = test(input)
print('output = ', output.cpu())

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
I need to train several neural networks with the same structure and with the same input. Training one by one takes quite a long time and I found that using model ensembling would be a good option here. However, when I try it, the models are not optimizing. I provide this simple example:
import torch as th
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.func import stack_module_state, functional_call

import sys

import copy

vectorized = False

class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.fc = nn.Linear(2,1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return th.sigmoid(self.fc(x))


models = [Net().to("cuda") for _ in range(1)]
models = nn.ModuleList(models)

optimizer = th.optim.Adam(models.parameters(), lr=0.05)

if vectorized:

    def fmodel(params, buffers, x):
        return functional_call(base_model, (params, buffers), x)


    for epoch in range(100):
        data = th.rand(1,2) * 2 - 1
        data = data.to("cuda")

        params, buffers = stack_module_state(models)

        base_model = copy.deepcopy(models[0])
        base_model = base_model.to('meta')

        loss = th.vmap(fmodel, in_dims=(0, 0, None))(params, buffers, data)
        
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

        print(loss.item())

else:

    for epoch in range(100):
        data = th.rand(1,2) * 2 - 1
        data = data.to("cuda")
        for model in models:
            loss = model(data)

            optimizer.zero_grad()
            loss.backward()
            optimizer.step()

            print(loss.item())

nodes.bodyText:
🐛 Describe the bug
The bug occurs when layers are created as instance attributes (e.g., self.conv1, self.bn1) before being passed into an nn.Sequential. In this case, load_state_dict shows unexpected behavior. The code snippet below demonstrates this issue by creating a main model alongside several client models with identical architecture. In a simulation of a typical Federated Learning setup, the client models' weights are averaged. The test_load_state_dict function tests whether loading these averaged weights into the main model results in correct or unexpected behavior.
Minified repro:
import copy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from typing import List, Dict

class BuggyNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels: int = 1):
        super(BuggyNet, self).__init__()
        self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        self.bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
        self.RELU = nn.ReLU()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(self.conv1, self.bn1, self.RELU)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = x
        out = self.net(out)
        return out
    
class OkayNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, in_channels: int = 1):
        super(OkayNet, self).__init__()
        conv1 = nn.Conv2d(
            in_channels, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1, bias=False
        )
        bn1 = nn.BatchNorm2d(32)
        RELU = nn.ReLU()
        self.net = nn.Sequential(conv1, bn1, RELU)

    def forward(self, x):
        out = x
        out = self.net(out)
        return out

def test_load_state_dict(trained_weights: Dict[str, torch.Tensor], main: nn.Module):
    main.load_state_dict(trained_weights)
    main_new_state_dict = main.state_dict()

    # compare loaded items
    properly_loaded = True
    for k1, v1 in trained_weights.items():
        v2 = main_new_state_dict[k1]

        if v1.ndim == 0:
            if torch.norm(v1 - v2, p=1) > 1e-6:
                print(
                    f"Wrong weights for key {k1}, norm_diff = {torch.norm(v2-v1, p=1)}"
                )
                properly_loaded = False
        elif not torch.allclose(v1, v2):
            print(f"Wrong weights for key {k1}, norm_diff = {torch.norm(v2-v1, p=1)}")
            properly_loaded = False

    if properly_loaded:
        print("[+] Correct behavior: Loaded weights match the weights that were meant to be loaded.")
    else:
        print(
            "[-] Unexpected behavior: Loaded weights are different from the weights that were meant to be loaded."
        )

@torch.no_grad()
def average_weights(weights: List[Dict[str, torch.Tensor]]) -> Dict[str, torch.Tensor]:
    weights_avg = copy.deepcopy(weights[0])

    for key in weights_avg.keys():
        for i in range(1, len(weights)):
            weights_avg[key] += weights[i][key]
        weights_avg[key] = torch.div(weights_avg[key], len(weights))
    return weights_avg


if __name__ == "__main__":
    num_clients = 2
    ### Bug experiment:
    buggy_main_model = BuggyNet()
    # average multiple clients
    client_models = [BuggyNet() for _ in range(num_clients)]
    buggy_avg_weights = average_weights([x.state_dict() for x in client_models])
    # Test if load_state_dict works properly
    test_load_state_dict(buggy_avg_weights, buggy_main_model)
    print("-" * 40)

    # ### Okay experiment:
    okay_main_model = OkayNet()
    client_models = [OkayNet() for _ in range(num_clients)]
    okay_avg_weights = average_weights([x.state_dict() for x in client_models])

    test_load_state_dict(okay_avg_weights, okay_main_model)
    print("-" * 40)

Wrong weights for key bn1.running_var, norm_diff = 16.0
[-] Unexpected behavior: Loaded weights are different from the weights that were meant to be loaded.
----------------------------------------
[+] Correct behavior: Loaded weights match the weights that were meant to be loaded.
----------------------------------------

I am working on robotics projects that need Linux OS and a GPU, and my setup is Mac M1 with Ubuntu 22.04 running via VMWare Fusion. I would like to use my host machine's GPU device on my virtual machine. I created a similar post almost a year ago for a more specific problem #97188.
Alternatives
I have little to no idea what I'm doing but here's what I've tried so far.
Trying to install the Stable (2.2.1) + Mac + Conda + Python + Default Pytorch package on my Ubuntu VM using conda install pytorch::pytorch torchvision torchaudio -c pytorch was unsuccessful with the following output

nodes.bodyText:
📚 The doc issue
The ReduceLROnPlateau learning rate scheduler doesn't have the get_last_lr() nor the print_lr functions that are mentioned in its documentation page.
Referred docs:
https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau.html#torch.optim.lr_scheduler.ReduceLROnPlateau.get_last_lr
Simple example:
import torch
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.optim.lr_scheduler import ReduceLROnPlateau

def loss_function():
    # Dummy loss calculation
    return torch.ones(1, requires_grad=True)

model = torch.nn.Linear(10, 2)
optimizer = optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)
scheduler = ReduceLROnPlateau(optimizer, 'min', patience=3)

# Dummy training loop
for epoch in range(10):
    for _ in range(100):
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss = loss_function()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
    
    validation_loss = loss_function().item()
    scheduler.step(validation_loss)
    
    print(scheduler.get_last_lr()) # <<< function doesn't exist
    # works: print(optimizer.param_groups[0]['lr'])
>>> AttributeError: 'ReduceLROnPlateau' object has no attribute 'get_last_lr'
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
The function should either be supported or removed from the docs.
For consistency, it would be best if it is supported as mentioned in the docs, for other schedulers (e.g. OneCycleLR) scheduler.get_last_lr() works.
nodes.title: ReduceLROnPlateau.get_last_lr() mentioned in docs doesn't exist
